terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, deponent, with accusative
evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.20 fin.: ingenium tuum, Crasse, vehementer admīrāns (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To regard with admiration, of a person, a talent, a deed; just as often to be surprised at something (admīrātus sum brevitātem epistulae, Cic. Att. 6.9), so the context decides. Admīrātiō is admiration, admīrābilis admirable (see wonderful).

evidence: Cic. Off. 2.36: eōs virōs suspiciunt maximīsque efferunt laudibus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally to look up at; of people, to look up to, the opposite of dēspicere. Its other common sense is to suspect, so make the context plain.
The plain verb for being surprised or amazed; it means admire only where the context makes the wonder approving.

phrases.latin: nīl admīrārī prope rēs est ūna, Numīcī, sōlaque quae possit facere et servāre beātum
phrases.english: to be dazzled by nothing, Numicius, is almost the one and only thing that can make a man happy and keep him so

phrases.latin: paulisper alter alterīus cōnspectū, admīrātiōne mūtuā prope attonitī, conticuēre
phrases.english: for a little while they were silent, almost stunned with admiration at the sight of each other

phrases.latin: eōs virōs suspiciunt maximīsque efferunt laudibus
phrases.english: such men they look up to and praise to the skies
